themes.theme: User reporting and escalation of suspect outputs to human review
themes.definition: Channels for users or staff to flag AI outputs that look wrong, biased, harmful or opaque, and the named people who act on those reports.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 says organisations should have 'systems in place that allow users to report issues and prompt a human review', and should nominate SROs 'responsible for monitoring reports and implementing adequate changes throughout the AI system's life cycle'. UK010 recommends 'governance mechanisms that allow users to escalate AI decisions when they appear incorrect, biased or opaque'. UK099 asks for user feedback and issue-reporting systems 'throughout the system's life', visible to users. AI_Insights lists a 'User feedback mechanism' as required at Medium risk. In this cell these are the only passages that describe how a particular output comes before a human: a user notices a problem and reports it. 'Users' is not defined consistently (the UK010 coder note reads it as either staff or affected people), and the passages do not say what the human reviewer checks against or what changes follow.
themes.holders: Public organisations deploying AI (provide the channel); SROs (monitor reports, UK174); users and affected people (report); organisations that use AI (UK010).
themes.binding: 'Should' or practical recommendation (UK174, UK099, UK010); 'required' at Medium risk in a non-binding guidance table (AI_Insights). Consequence: not stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: a user report or escalation after an output is produced. Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: an unnamed human reviewer; SROs monitor reports (UK174). What happens with the result: 'a human review' and 'adequate changes' (UK174); otherwise not stated. Which cases reach a human: only those a user reports or escalates; no sampling, confidence-score routing or category of output that must always be reviewed is stated in this cell.

themes.definition: Duties to report security incidents, data breaches, misuse or suspected unauthorised behaviour of AI tools through internal or contractual channels, and to plan when incidents are disclosed to the public.
themes.what_is_set_out: DWP is the most specific (UK190): all users must ensure misuse of AI tools is reported to their line manager and, if required, the Security Incident Response Team; users must report security incidents through the Security Incident Referral Webform; anyone aware of a breach of policy should notify the Security Policy and Standards team; suppliers must raise incidents and data breaches with the DWP Contract Manager and report abuse of AI tools; and contract managers must report supplier abuse through the DWP Place portal. UK136 says the application 'must have an easy way to report any suspected unauthorised behaviour to relevant authorities within or outside the organisation', without naming them. UK099 asks teams to prepare answers in advance, including who investigates breaches and 'how will you inform impacted users of a breach?'; UK071 recommends an incident response plan covering 'Who investigates?, What triggers rollback?, When is public disclosure needed?'. Only DWP attaches a consequence (discipline, next theme); the others leave the recipient and the criteria for public disclosure open.
themes.holders: DWP users, line managers, suppliers and their third parties, and contract managers; any individual aware of a breach (UK190); the buying department and supplier (UK136); project teams (UK099, UK071).
themes.binding: Mandatory by DWP policy ('must'), with discipline for failure to report; 'must' in procurement guidance (UK136); questions and recommendations elsewhere.
themes.checks: Trigger: a suspected or actual incident, breach or misuse ('as soon as possible' in DWP, per coder note). Compared against: DWP security policy and standards. Metric or threshold: not stated; criteria for rollback and public disclosure are to be planned but are not given (UK071). Who: users, suppliers and contract managers report; the Security Incident Response Team and Security Policy and Standards team receive. What happens with the result: investigation, possible rollback and public disclosure (UK071), informing affected users (UK099); otherwise not stated.

quotes.quote: It is the responsibility of all users to ensure that misuse of AI tools is reported to their line manager and, if required, to the Security Incident Response Team

themes.definition: Stated consequences for failing to meet AI-related duties: internal discipline, regulatory penalties, personal liability and the risk of legal challenge.
themes.what_is_set_out: Few documents state any consequence. DWP says line managers act on non-compliance 'as detailed in the DWP Discipline Policy', that failure to report a security incident 'could result in disciplinary action and, in the most severe circumstances, result in dismissal', that all staff and suppliers using DWP devices must comply with its security policies, and that its standards of behaviour apply to AI use (UK190). Ofgem ties its existing enforcement powers to AI: penalties of up to 10% of turnover, consumer redress orders, disqualification of directors for competition breaches, personal responsibility of IT directors and managers, and the rule that a breach 'derived from the use of AI does not excuse or mitigate breach' (UK010); these apply to energy licensees and regulated persons, not to public bodies using AI [inference]. For public bodies, the consequences named are those of general law: UK216 warns of 'reputational damage and legal action' under the Equality Act and the PSED and says a body 'should be able to justify' narrowing its equality analysis 'if you are challenged'; UK174 notes possible legal challenge on public-law grounds (coder note). AI_Insights says 'Failure to adequately protect our users is a breach of duty' without naming the duty's source. Across the cell, 'if not met: not stated' is the norm.
themes.holders: DWP users, employees, suppliers and line managers; Ofgem (enforcer) and energy licensees, regulated persons, IT directors and managers; public bodies in England (UK216); public bodies under public law (UK174); creators and users of generative AI (AI_Insights).
themes.binding: DWP: mandatory policy with discipline and dismissal. Ofgem: statutory enforcement powers over the energy sector. UK216 and UK174: consequences of existing statute and public law, restated in guidance. AI_Insights: a statement of duty with no cited source.

quotes.quote: Failure to report a security incident, potential or otherwise, could result in disciplinary action and, in the most severe circumstances, result in dismissal.
under existing enforcement powers Ofgem can impose financial penalties of up to 10% of a regulated person’s turnover in sectoral matters.

Failure to adequately protect our users is a breach of duty.

themes.theme: Supplier and supply-chain responsibility and liability
themes.definition: How responsibility, liability, and duties to explain or report are allocated to suppliers, vendors and developers outside the public body, mainly through contracts.
themes.what_is_set_out: Contracts are the main tool. UK174: 'Where AI is bought commercially, define detailed responsibilities and liability contractually', and make sure all parties, 'from vendors and technical teams to system users', understand their legal obligations. UK099 lists responsibilities to write into contracts, including product liability where the system 'gives unsafe outcomes or fails', with penalties, clawback and termination for suppliers (coder note), and says vendors 'must be able to clearly explain' how their tools work and generate outputs. UK136 places liability for use, data access and transfer with the department and 'technical, security and quality assurance' with the supplier, and lets buyers ask suppliers for 'Processes to ensure accountability over outputs of algorithms'; UK010 wants AI risks 'appropriately allocated in contractual arrangements along the supply chain'. DWP binds its suppliers directly: they 'must be transparent when using AI tools for DWP business', including evidence of how AI output was achieved (UK190). UK216 says a third party delivering a service 'may be subject to the PSED' while the duty stays with the public body, which should 'monitor compliance'; UK268 says the auditee must document compliance even where it cannot see a bought-in system's code. UK139 notes that some regulators can assign legal responsibility only to deployers, leaving developers to 'non-statutory measures', and that deployers can contest outcomes with developers. The pattern across documents is that the public body keeps responsibility (theme 2) while suppliers carry contractual liability; the ATRS adds public disclosure of which supplier is responsible for which part (UK086), and UK085 expects suppliers to accept public-sector transparency. UK207 says supply-chain actors need to understand 'their accountabilities' but does not allocate them.
themes.holders: Public bodies as buyers (write and enforce contract terms); suppliers, vendors and their third parties (bear liability, explain, report); AI developers and deployers (UK139); third parties delivering services (UK216).
themes.binding: Recommended contract terms ('should', 'may also need to'); DWP's supplier duties are mandatory by policy; the PSED itself is statutory but its reach to third parties is stated as 'may'. Consequence for suppliers: contractual penalties, clawback and termination (UK099, per coder note); otherwise not stated.
themes.checks: n/a. Bears on outputs only in that suppliers may be asked for 'Processes to ensure accountability over outputs of algorithms' (UK136) or for evidence of how AI output was achieved (UK190); what those processes check is not stated.

themes.theme: Answering to regulators and central government
themes.definition: Routes by which a public body or other organisation must report to, consult or satisfy a regulator or a central government control about its AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 restates that where a DPIA shows a high risk that cannot be reduced, 'you must consult the ICO before you can start processing personal data', and that AI spending can fall under the Digital and technology spend control's 'functional assurance of central government spending'. UK010 asks energy-sector stakeholders to 'assure themselves, and competition authorities' that AI is not anti-competitive, and says Ofgem 'may take adherence to standards and frameworks into account when assessing compliance'. UK206 presents AI assurance as how organisations 'demonstrate this to government, regulators, and the market'. UK082 recommends that sponsor departments 'demonstrate how they are funding this capability within their budgets through the Spending Review process'. Only the ICO consultation is a statutory duty with a stated effect (processing cannot start until it happens); the others are guidance or recommendations with no consequence stated.
themes.holders: Public organisations processing personal data (to the ICO); buying organisations (to central government spend control); energy-sector stakeholders (to Ofgem and competition authorities); organisations generally (UK206); sponsor departments (to the Spending Review, [inference] HM Treasury).
themes.binding: ICO prior consultation: statutory, restated. Spend control: mandatory by policy where it applies. Others: 'should', 'can' or recommendation. Consequence: processing cannot start without ICO consultation [inference from 'before you can start']; otherwise not stated.

quotes.location: Using AI safely and responsibly > Data protection…
quotes.quote: you’re unable to sufficiently reduce these risks despite mitigating actions, you must consult the ICO before you can start processing personal data.
stakeholders should be able to assure themselves, and competition authorities, that the system containing AI is not operating in an anti-competitive manner.
Through AI assurance, organisations can measure whether systems are trustworthy and demonstrate this to government, regulators, and the market.
Government should also ensure all sponsor departments demonstrate how they are funding this capability within their budgets through the Spending Review process.

themes.theme: Regulators' role and remit in holding AI to account
themes.definition: What regulators are asked or empowered to do about AI accountability: assign legal responsibility, require information, audit and inspect, enforce, and publish their own approach.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK139, guidance to regulators, is written as considerations and questions: whether their 'regulatory powers or remits allow them to place legal responsibility on actors in the supply chain that are best placed to mitigate the risks'; where responsibility for AI outcomes sits in their remit; clarifying the responsibilities of developers and deployers, which 'could include ... sharing documentation on key decisions and allowing audits where appropriate'; and 'asking or requiring (under existing powers)' information on how they meet the transparency principle. It also states a limit: a regulator's role in holding developers and deployers 'to account legally is also contingent on whether they are a regulated entity within that regulators' remit', and some vertical regulators may reach only deployers. UK139 encourages regulators to publish their strategic approach to AI and reminds them of their own Equality Act and Human Rights Act duties. UK082 recommends requiring all regulators 'to publish annually how they have enabled innovation and growth driven by AI in their sector', with transparent metrics. UK207 mentions regulators 'auditing and inspecting AI as part of their enforcement activity', and UK010 sets out Ofgem's enforcement toolkit as it applies to AI. Note the direction of UK082's duty: regulators would answer publicly for enabling AI-driven growth, not for how they constrain AI.
themes.holders: Regulators (consider, ask, require, publish); AI developers and deployers within their remit (answer to them); Ofgem as a named regulator.
themes.binding: Non-binding guidance to regulators ('consider', 'could', 'encouraged'); UK082 is a recommendation with no recorded acceptance in the coded text; Ofgem's powers are statutory. Consequence: depends on each regulator's powers, which are not stated except for Ofgem.

quotes.quote: Consider whether regulators’ regulatory powers or remits allow them to place legal responsibility on actors in the supply chain that are best placed to mitigate the risks.
A regulators’ role in holding AI developers and AI deployers to account legally is also contingent on whether they are a regulated entity within that regulators’ remit.
Require all regulators to publish annually how they have enabled innovation and growth driven by AI in their sector.
Beyond auditing and inspecting AI as part of their enforcement activity, regulators will play an important role in supporting the development of the broader AI assurance ecosystem.

themes.theme: Existing law restated as accountability duties
themes.definition: Passages that restate duties from existing law (UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, the Equality Act 2010 and the Public Sector Equality Duty, public law, the Human Rights Act) as part of accountability for AI.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK GDPR duties appear most often: transparency about automated decision-making and its logic, and rights of access, correction and objection (UK174); meeting 'your legal duties under the UK General Data Protection Regulation', including DPIAs and showing how the principles are met (UK099); privacy information on purposes, retention and sharing, and opt-out and erasure 'where legally required' (UK010); and general compliance (UK206). UK216 says the PSED 'applies even if' the body commissions or buys an AI tool or has a third party use it on its behalf, and that failure may bring legal action. UK268 restates that public sector organisations 'must be transparent in their decision-making', including decisions 'supported or made by AI systems', and reads anti-discrimination law as possibly reaching group-level statistical disadvantage. UK174 summarises public-law principles (acting rationally, fairly, lawfully and compatibly with human rights), UK206 says systems 'must adhere to existing regulation such as UK GDPR, the Equality Act 2010', and UK139 reminds regulators of their Equality Act and Human Rights Act duties. These passages carry statutory force, but the documents restate rather than create the duties, and they rarely name who enforces them.
themes.holders: Data controllers; public bodies and public sector organisations; organisations processing data; regulators as public bodies (UK139); third parties delivering services on a public body's behalf (UK216, 'may').
themes.binding: Statutory duties restated in non-statutory guidance; UK268's reading of anti-discrimination law is a non-binding interpretation. Consequence: legal action and reputational damage (UK216); legal challenge (UK174, coder note); otherwise not stated. Enforcers are not named in the passages ([inference] the ICO, the EHRC and the courts).

themes.theme: The wider assurance ecosystem: accreditation, certification and civil society
themes.definition: Actors outside government and the deploying body (third-party assurance providers, accreditation bodies, certification or 'kitemarking', civil society) that check AI systems or check those who check them.
themes.what_is_set_out: UK206 says 'A range of actors need to check that AI systems are trustworthy and compliant, and to communicate evidence of this to others', names accreditation bodies (UKAS) to attest to 'the ongoing competence, impartiality' of third-party assurance providers against international standards, and says civil society organisations 'can support multi-stakeholder feedback and scrutiny on AI systems'. UK207 says an approach like 'auditing or kitemarking in other sectors will be needed' so that businesses, consumers and regulators can know whether AI systems are 'effective, trustworthy and legal', and that accreditation builds trust by 'checking the checkers'; the coder note records that it treats the model as not yet chosen ('too early to tell'). These passages describe roles and aspirations for a market, not duties on public bodies, and do not say whether public-sector AI must use accredited or certified assurance.
themes.holders: Third-party assurance providers; accreditation bodies including UKAS; civil society organisations; 'a range of actors'.
themes.binding: Descriptive role statements and aspirations ('need to', 'can support', 'will be needed'). Consequence: not stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: not stated ('ongoing' competence for accreditation). Compared against: international standards (accreditation of assurance providers). Metric or threshold: not stated. Who: accreditation bodies over assurance providers; assurance providers over AI systems. What happens with the result: not stated.

quotes.quote: A range of actors need to check that AI systems are trustworthy and compliant, and to communicate evidence of this to others.
Through oversight and stakeholder convening, civil society organisations can support multi-stakeholder feedback and scrutiny on AI systems.
A similar approach to auditing or ‘kitemarking’ in other sectors will be needed to enable businesses, consumers and regulators to know whether the AI systems are effective, trustworthy and legal.
Accreditation schemes build trust in the ecosystem by ‘checking the checkers’ to ensure those providing assurance services are competent to do so.

themes.definition: Passages that make the strength of an accountability measure (explanation, audit, appeal route, external audit, audit trail) depend on the risk level or public exposure of the AI system.
themes.what_is_set_out: AI_Insights' bias risk matrix is the most explicit: a 'User feedback mechanism' at Medium risk, a 'Regulatory compliance audit' at High risk, and a 'User appeal mechanism', 'Complete audit trail' and 'Monthly external audit' at Critical risk, on the reasoning that 'External exposure creates accountability to users, regulators, and the public that internal tools do not face'. UK071 says high-risk AI, such as systems that 'could endanger lives or cause legal determinations about individuals', demands 'exhaustive testing, possibly including formal verification or external audits before deployment'. UK268 makes explainability 'proportionate to the risk' and audit depth 'determined by the risks connected to the AI system'; UK010 requires grid-management AI to be explainable 'in a manner that is proportionate to the risk'. The documents do not share a risk scale, which produces a tension: an appeal route is a 'must' for any AI decision in UK174 and a 'must' in UK099, but is required only at Critical risk in AI_Insights.
themes.holders: Not stated in the AI_Insights table (the operator of the application [inference]); unnamed for UK071's high-risk testing; auditors for audit depth (UK268); energy-sector stakeholders (UK010).
themes.binding: 'Required' in a non-binding guidance table (AI_Insights); 'possibly' (UK071); good practice (UK268); 'duty' as stated (UK010). Consequence: not stated.
themes.checks: Trigger: the risk level assigned to the system (AI_Insights Medium, High and Critical; UK071 'high-risk'); before deployment for UK071's external audits; monthly at Critical risk (AI_Insights). Compared against: not stated. Metric or threshold: the risk tier decides which measures apply; how a system is placed in a tier is outside these passages. Who: not stated; the external auditor is unnamed. What happens with the result: not stated.

not_themed.reason: A reflective question in UK099 ('are you following a particular mandate or requirement to be transparent?') among prompts on why to be transparent. It is on topic but sets out no requirement, holder, mechanism or recipient, so it adds nothing to any theme's substance.

absences: Every starting code for Accountability has passages: named accountable roles, sign-off, publication, registration (ATRS, plus internal agent inventories), reporting to regulators or boards, audit, complaint and redress, and sanctions. Two are thin. Sanctions: the only stated consequences are DWP's internal discipline and Ofgem's enforcement powers over energy licensees; nothing is stated for a public body that fails to publish an ATRS record, skips sign-off or offers no appeal route. Reporting to regulators: only the restated ICO prior consultation is a duty with a stated effect. Things a reader would expect that the passages do not give: (1) to whom a named role (SRO, data owner, AI asset owner, board) answers and what happens to it if things go wrong, which is 'not stated' almost everywhere; (2) any line of answerability to Parliament or ministers, apart from ministerial clearance of ATRS records 'in certain high-profile instances' (Parliament appears only in a coder note on the NAO); (3) an external body that hears AI complaints (no ombudsman or tribunal is named; UK139 points to 'existing routes' without naming them), and any timescale or defined remedy for an appeal; (4) a duty to publish audit findings or evaluation results (UK133 does not require publication), or any monitoring of ATRS compliance; (5) on checking AI outputs, no accuracy, consistency or repeatability measure or threshold, no confidence scores, and no requirement to record prompts. Model versions appear only in UK071 (version metadata and archiving) and UK133 (name the model used); the ATRS leaves the model sections blank for off-the-shelf LLMs the organisation has not tested or refined. Which outputs reach a human is set only by user reports and escalation, and by auditors checking that human review exists; there is no rule on sampling outputs or on categories of output that must always be reviewed.
cross_cutting: This cell is dominated by transparency and the naming of responsibility: the ATRS (who must publish, what a record must say, how it is cleared) and statements that the public body, its SRO and its staff own AI outputs together account for a large share of the passages, alongside the SAI audit guide's long list of what auditors should examine. Most of it is non-statutory guidance; the only firm duties are the ATRS for central government departments and in-scope arm's length bodies (policy, not statute), DWP's internal policy with discipline attached, and existing law restated (UK GDPR, the Equality Act and PSED, the ICO prior consultation). Consequences are the thinnest part: the documents say clearly who is responsible but almost never to whom that person answers or what follows a failure, and the only concrete sanctions are DWP discipline and Ofgem penalties that apply to energy companies rather than to public bodies [inference]. The holder is usually 'you', meaning the public organisation or project team, with SROs, boards and audit committees inside it; outside it, the NAO and SAIs, regulators (whose reach depends on their remit) and suppliers bound by contract. Several documents in the cell are not addressed to public bodies using AI: UK010 to energy-sector stakeholders, UK139 to regulators, and UK206 and UK207 to the assurance market. Their passages are themed here, but their holders differ from those of the government-wide guidance. On checking AI outputs, the cell assigns responsibility for outputs firmly to the deploying body and its users, but the means of checking sit elsewhere: auditors may run or reproduce models and confirm that human review happens (UK268); two technical sources ask for output logs, version metadata and threshold records (AI_Insights, UK071); and the ATRS asks bodies to disclose testing they have done rather than requiring it. No passage sets an accuracy or consistency threshold, and the only stated route by which a specific output reaches a human is a user reporting or escalating it.
